Let’s talk about something we all face at some point—conflict.
This is Chapter 8: Navigating Conflict and Repair.
No matter how much healing you’ve done, conflict is just part of being human. Old wounds can get triggered, misunderstandings pop up, and—let’s be honest—sometimes we hurt each other, even when we don’t mean to. But what really matters isn’t the conflict itself, it’s what you do next.
Imagine a dad who snaps at his teenage son during an argument. Right away, he feels that old rush of shame. In the past, he might’ve just pulled away, hoping things would smooth over on their own. But this time, he remembers what he’s learned about repair. So, he finds his son in the kitchen, takes a slow breath, and says, “I’m sorry. I lost my temper. That wasn’t fair to you.”
At first, his son just shrugs. But the dad sees something shift—the boy’s shoulders drop, just a bit. Suddenly, the air between them doesn’t feel so heavy.
Here’s something to pay attention to: repair isn’t about pretending the hurt never happened. It’s about recognizing it. When you step up and take responsibility for your actions, you help the other person’s body relax. Their nervous system, which is always on the lookout for danger, gets the message—hey, it’s safe to reconnect.
Now, this isn’t just for families. In communities, repair might mean honest conversations, real apologies, or even changing how things are done. Think about a school principal who hears from students that they don’t feel listened to. Instead of brushing it off, she starts regular listening sessions. Sure, the students are wary at first. But little by little, they start to believe that their voices actually matter.
So what does all this tell us? Conflict isn’t a sign you’ve failed—it’s a chance to grow. When you handle it with care, it can actually build more trust and make your relationships stronger.
The real key? Stay present. Listen closely. Be willing to make things right.
